source.title: Closed Gates Leak: Decomposing Adjacent-Layer Cancellation in Gated Language Models

page_placements.theme: Counterbalancing in ordinary forward passes: later components partly cancel or damp earlier writes and confident predictions, with no ablation

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures adjacent-layer residual-stream cancellation and its mechanism, but does not measure the claim versions’ attention-component ablation and prediction-recovery behavior. It discusses self-repair and argues that this cancellation does not establish selective feature rejection.
record.gate_note: The paper’s counterfactual removes a layer’s write from the next MLP’s input and measures directional damping and adjacent-layer contribution cosines. Those are related to, but do not measure, restoration of the original prediction after ablating an attention layer or head. The study also reports many training, intervention, Jacobian, and activation results; the rows below focus on its principal per-model decomposition and the per-model comparison of damping directions. Values used only to select settings are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures adjacent-layer residual cancellation: the next MLP's damping of the previous layer's write, and the cosine between adjacent contributions. It never ablates an attention layer or head and measures recovery of the output or logits. It does not measure late-MLP downregulation of the top token, and it does not test the named self-repair mechanisms. Self-repair (McGrath et al.; Rushing & Nanda) appears only in related work. There the authors note that by the definition of D, removing layer j−1's write makes the next MLP write more along it. That is a residual-direction response, not prediction restoration, so the paper discusses the claim without testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that adjacent-layer cancellation in gated models comes from an average contraction carried by closed-gate strengthening neurons, not from selective rejection of the previous write. Hence cancellation is weak evidence about which features a model rejects. They support this with interventions: annealing the negative gate region removes damping and cancellation in two models.
record.recipe_differences: The study decomposes adjacent-layer residual contributions using a counterfactual removal of the prior write from the next MLP’s input, and analyzes gated-MLP damping. It does not ablate attention layers or heads and measure restoration of the output prediction.
record.method_sensitivity: The sign and magnitude of adjacent-layer cosine can depend on the measurement frame and controls; the text notes this for Phi-3-mini, Gemma-2B, and ProSparse-7B. The study also reports differences between controlled and raw write directions.

fits_no_version.finding: In ten gated models the next MLP damps the previous layer's write (D 0.118 to 0.497 per unit). This damping is carried mostly by closed-gate strengthening neurons (71% to 140% of D). The previous write is damped less than the same layer's write at another token (ratio 0.88 to 0.99). Annealing the gate's negative region away in continued pretraining removes both the damping and the cancellation in Qwen2.5-0.5B and Llama-3.2-1B. By construction, removing the previous write makes the next MLP write more along it. This is a non-selective, MLP-level response to a removed write, measured in the residual direction rather than on the output.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gated MLPs contract, on average over directions, whatever they read, through the leaky negative region of SiLU/GELU gates. Removing an earlier layer's write therefore raises the next MLP's write along it, without singling that write out.

record.problems: The main measurements use sixteen documents from one corpus at 192 tokens, with intervals over documents within that corpus. The authors report checks on a second corpus, longer sequences, and 64 documents. Continued-pretraining interventions cover two models, with three seeds for Qwen2.5-0.5B and one for Llama-3.2-1B. The study does not measure the output-prediction recovery behavior in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported model-specific results are not extracted here, including neuron-group damping, mean damping over random directions, lag-2 and lag-3 decompositions, training trajectories, closed-side annealing, activation thresholding, converted ReLU models, and Jacobian-spectrum analyses (Sections 3–5 and Appendices B–J). They concern the paper’s adjacent-layer cancellation mechanism rather than the claim versions’ attention-ablation prediction recovery.

untested.parts: No attention-layer ablation, and no measurement of later attention layers restoring the output.
No late-MLP downregulation of the maximum-likelihood token, and no change in it after earlier ablation.
No single-head ablation, and no full-distribution compensation measure.
No per-prompt compensation or overcorrection of an ablation effect. The directional spread of damping (Appendix G) is a different quantity.
No backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final-LayerNorm rescaling or anti-erasure neurons tested. Closed-gate strengthening neurons explain adjacent-layer damping, not self-repair.
No mean or resample ablation of components with a recovery measure. Removing the previous write from the MLP input is the study's own counterfactual, not a comparison of ablation types.
Ablation-based importance scores are not evaluated. The paper's implication about reading layer contributions is stated as untested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's rows and their 'none' links are correct. All twenty rows measure directional damping or adjacent cosines, which no version names, so cannot_determine is appropriate. Row values match Tables 4 and 9. Table 9's ratio column lists write:random 1.20 for Phi-3-mini and 0.96 for Gemma-2B, as recorded. No labels are given because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: No attention-layer ablation followed by later attention-layer compensation or restoration of the original output prediction is measured.
No late-MLP maximum-likelihood-token downregulation or its change after earlier-component ablation is measured.
No single-head ablation or full-distribution compensation across prompts, model families, or sizes is measured.
The paper measures variation in directional damping, not prompt-level variation or overcorrection of an ablation’s effect on the original prediction.

The study identifies closed-gate strengthening neurons as a source of adjacent-layer damping, but does not test the named backup-head, copy-suppression-head, final-LayerNorm, or anti-erasure-neuron mechanisms in this version.
The interventions alter gated-MLP activation functions or threshold activations; they are not on-distribution ablations of attention components using mean or resample activations.
The paper does not test whether ablation-based importance scores misstate a component’s contribution.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B
rows.operation_detail: Removed the previous layer’s write from the next MLP’s input to decompose its projected contribution.
rows.measure: Counterfactual damping D and adjacent-layer contribution cosine in the controlled frame
rows.baseline: A+C, the attention and MLP contribution along the previous write when that write is absent from the next MLP’s input
rows.uncertainty: 95% interval over documents for D; cosine interval not stated
rows.note: The negative residual contribution indicates adjacent-layer cancellation in this measurement; the study does not measure output-prediction restoration after component ablation.

relation.reason: The related-work discussion connects damping to self-repair and erasure, but the study neither tests a listed version nor uses self-repair as a tool.

tranche.reason: Measures adjacent-layer cancellation and gated-MLP contraction, without testing output recovery, maximum-likelihood-token counterbalancing, or attribution errors specified by the claim versions.

source_check.notes: The reported A+C totals are arithmetic sums of Table 4's separately printed A and C cells. The synthesis statement's ten-model range and mechanism shares are supported, although r1–r5 alone do not cover all ten models.
